newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian villagers release last Shell hostages.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian villagers release last Shell hostages.

text.p: Nigerian villagers who took hostage Shell oil workers last week in a political dispute with the government released the last 52 of their captives on Thursday, a Shell spokesman said.

"All our staff and contractors are now back safely in Warri," said the spokesman for the Anglo-Dutch giant Royal Dutch/Shell in Lagos. The midwestern oil city of Warri is headquarters of Shell's operations in the western sector of Nigeria.

Ijaw tribesmen seized Shell's oil flow stations on Saturday in the midwestern Delta state and held 127 Nigerian staff hostages in protest against the government's relocation of their local government headquarters from Ijaw area.
Many of the hostages had been freed by Wednesday night after delicate negotiations with the communities.
In the first official action on the crisis, navy chief Rear-Admiral Mike Akhigbe met Ijaw community leaders in Warri on Thursday for four hours and urged them to stop the action.

"I want to appeal to you to help restore normalcy, law and order in the communities and to allow government time and space to look into your grievances," said Akhigbe, who comes from the same part of Nigeria and is a member of the military government's ruling council.
The Shell spokesman said there had been no conditions set by the villagers for freeing the company's staff. "All they asked was that we should pass on their grievances to the government."
Three Ijaw tribesmen died in the protests that escalated into riots in Warri on Tuesday and forced the reduction in Shell's oil output in the area.
Shell officials in Warri said resuming production in the occupied stations would depend on the state of the facilities.
"With peace now prevailing we will be able to assess the facilities and if they are not vandalised we can resume output very soon," said one.
In Warri, the freed Shell oil workers said on Thursday they were beaten by their captors and threatened with death.

"A group of 40 Ijaws armed with automatic rifles, cudgels and crude implements attacked the Egwa flow station in flying boats and disarmed the lone policeman," said a station attendant who was among the nearly 80 hostages freed earlier.
"They flogged me with cutlasses, threatening to kill me... I'll never go back there," said another. Both declined to be identified for fear of reprisals from the community.
The cause of the problem is a rivalry in the Warri area between three tribes -- the Ijaws, the Itsekiris and Urhobohs.
The Urhobohs controlled the affairs in the oil town in the 1970s until the following decade when the Itsekiris, who provide the ruler for Warri, began to press for more say in the town.
The Ijaws, who inhabit the riverine areas and have a bigger population, also began asking for more amenities in their areas.

"There is a deep-rooted rivalry among the three tribes," said John Nana, a lawyer of Urhoboh-Itsekiri parentage. "People feel that if a local government is sited in their town then they get more government patronage by way of amenities."

Output has also been cut in Nembe in the southeast, where villagers protesting against the merger of two communities into one local government also seized Shell flow stations and ordered its staff out of the facility.
The political grievances of the villagers against the military government caught the country's oil giant Royal Dutch/Shell in the middle and threatened a possible disruption in vital oil exports.
The closures have cut Shell's production by 210,000 barrels per day, about 10 percent of Nigeria's overall output,

Shell, which produces about half the country's daily output of 2.15 million barrels, and state-owned Nigerian National Petroleum Corp (NNPC) had said exports would be disrupted if the disturbances did not end soon.
